show: Between The Covers : Conversations with Writers in Fiction, Nonfiction & Poetry
titel: Milkweed Live : Creature Needs with Thalia Field, David Naimon & Anne de Marcken
einzeiler: Writers discuss animal conservation, science, and art via the anthology Creature Needs.
kurzfassung: Authors discuss the intersection of literature and scientific research in the anthology Creature Needs. They examine how scientific frameworks and narrative conventions shape human understanding of nature and other species. The conversation also explores writing practices, the role of imagination, and the complexities of human-animal relationships.
stichpunkte: Discussion centers on the anthology Creature Needs, pairing writers with scientific studies on basic survival needs.
Talia Field reads from her contribution Jump Scare, which uses screenplay formats to interrogate scientific logic and fear tropes.
David Naimon reads from his piece in the water section, blending anatomical details of hearing with a fictional narrative about a poet-naturalist.
The participants critique the illusion of objectivity and the removal of the human observer in scientific studies.
They discuss how traditional narrative forms often center human experience and heroism at the expense of broader ecological awareness.
The conversation addresses the role of art in service of ideas and the necessity of bringing imagination into ecological discourse.
Audience questions cover topics including characterization, the unknowability of animal consciousness, and overcoming imposter syndrome.

kapitel.titel: Discussion on Form, Narrative, and Science

clips.hook: Can a collection of literary works serve as a call to action?
clips.text: The speakers introduce the anthology as a polyvocal response to animal extinction that combines literature and scientific research to inspire change.

clips.hook: When does the drive for complete information become a barrier to progress?
clips.text: A quoted perspective questions whether prioritizing large-scale systemic analysis and complete data collection acts as an obstacle to transformative differences.

clips.hook: Challenging the bias that requires proof for animal empathy
clips.text: It is noted that science historically placed the burden of proof on demonstrating that animals have emotions, reflecting an unexamined human-centric story.

clips.hook: What is your preferred method for connecting with the non-human world?
clips.text: The moderator poses a question about intentional or incidental ways of de-centering oneself and engaging with the natural world.

clips.hook: Could the harsh realities of nature be communicated through sound?
clips.text: A participant reflects on whether audiences could tolerate experiencing the overwhelming sound of pain present in the natural world.

beschreibung:
Today’s conversation between Thalia Field and David Naimon, moderated by Anne de Marcken, was recorded in February as part of the Pacific Northwest College of Art’s Visual Arts low residency MFA program. Thalia and David discuss and explore their pieces within the anthology Creature Needs: Writers Respond to the Science of Animal Conservation, where each writer was given a scientific study to engage with and create art in relation to. As a result, side-blotched lizards, boreal toads and the green cutthroat trout all help make up the cross-species chorus of today’s conversation, one that isn’t just about making art in relation to science, but also about interrogating, through art-making, the assumptions baked into the scientific frame, and using art to reveal the unexamined stories hidden within that frame. Looking at other non-normative modes of scientific inquiry, ones where the line isn’t so bright between art and science, nor the subjective and the so-called objective, Thalia, David and Anne explore the various possibilities and pitfalls for art-makers and writers when engaging with the more-than-human world.
